canonical_question: What specific milling atmosphere (e.g., Ar, N2, vacuum) was used for the MA powder, and could nitrogen co-contamination occur?

question_variants.question: What specific milling atmosphere (e.g., Ar, N2, vacuum) was used for the MA powder, and could nitrogen co-contamination occur?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The MA powder was prepared in an Argon (Ar) atmosphere. While not explicitly labeled as 'nitrogen co-contamination', the text confirms oxygen incorporation due to the high surface area of the nanocrystalline particles during milling in Ar.

answers.answer: The MA powder was prepared using high energy ball milling in an Ar atmosphere for 42 h. The text notes that oxygen was incorporated into the powder due to the high surface area of the nanocrystalline particles, but does not mention nitrogen co-contamination.
answers.conditions: high energy ball milling, Ar atmosphere, 42 h
answers.mechanism: Oxygen incorporated due to high surface area of nanocrystalline powder particles
answers.boundary_limitation: No specific mention of nitrogen contamination levels or detection limits for N in the milling atmosphere context.
evidence_spans: MA powder prepared from the elemental powders (granularity −325 mesh) by high energy ball milling in an Ar atmosphere for 42 h using tungsten carbide balls.
The mean particle size of the MA powder was ≈3 μm and MA particles consisted of nanocrystalline grains
MA and AT powders were compacted by SPS in an SPS 10-4 device (Santa Rosa, California, CA, USA) using a graphite die (Ø 20 mm) and punches to compact the powder using pressure of 80 MPa.

source_evidence_spans: Oxygen was incorporated into the MA powder obviously during high energy ball milling due to high surface area of nanocrystalline powder particles
